During an incident, the on-call engineer opens the log search and filters on
. Nothing comes back, even though the payment service logs every step. A full-text search finds the line: "Payment declined for order 81723: card_declined". The code that wrote it used
, so the log store received a finished sentence and no
field. The dashboard meant to count declines by reason has the same problem: there's no
field to group on, and every message text is unique.
The belief: passing an interpolated string to
is the same as using a template with placeholders, just more readable. Both produce the same message, and interpolation is checked by the compiler.
The belief is understandable. In the console, the two calls really do print identical lines. String interpolation is the modern C# idiom, and IDEs offer to convert
calls into it. The template syntax, with braces and arguments after it, looks like
with names, a style many developers have been taught to replace.
But a log entry isn't only a line of text. With a template, the logger receives the text's structure; with interpolation, the structure is gone before the logger is called.
A template travels as a constant plus named values
LogWarning("Payment declined for order {OrderId}: {Reason}", orderId, reason)
and the values separately. The logger keeps them as key-value pairs:

Interpolation formats before the logger sees anything
runs. The logger receives a "template" with no placeholders and no values. In the same test, its state held a single entry:

, containing the full sentence. There's nothing to filter on, and because the template differs for every order, nothing to group by either. That's exactly what CA2254 flags: the association between placeholder names and their values is lost.
